items.title: Driving comfort and motion sickness incidence in an active tilting vehicle
items.abstract: Engaging in non-driving related tasks while using self-driving vehicles will increase the risk of motion sickness symptoms. Therefore, future on-board technological solutions should mitigate motion sickness. This study examines comfort and motion sickness in an active tilting vehicle, which aligns the passenger to the inside of the curve, increasing motion compensation. Subjective and physiological data from 22 participants were collected. A reduction in lateral acceleration experienced by 29% was detected in slalom and traffic circles, but subjective evaluation suggests that the active tilt is unfamiliar to passengers. No significant subjective or objective improvements in motion sickness correlates were detected, which contradicts established hypotheses regarding the effectiveness of active counter-movements of body and head. However, there were indications that participants with a higher motion sickness susceptibility were significantly more sensitive to changes during the ride, which may suggest that certain countermeasure require longer adaptation periods. • Real-world study of comfort and motion sickness in an active tilting car. • Active tilting showed no reduction in motion sickness incidence. • Motion sick passengers are more sensitive to active tilting. • Unfamiliar side effects may outweigh active tilt’s potential benefits.

items.title: Functional Support from AI: Investigating Preferences of Young Adults for Support Types Provided by AI Chatbots Around Sexual Risks and Abuse
items.abstract: As young people navigate complex online experiences, they may utilize Artificial Intelligence chatbots for support. Despite research on online support, young adults’ chatbot preferences for sexually sensitive topics remain under-explored., We surveyed 18 to 24-year-olds regarding their preferred chatbot support responses within real-world sexual risk scenarios: nonconsensual image sharing, sexual abuse, and peer pressure. Participants were unaware that responses varied across five support types: informational, functional, esteem, network, and emotional. We compared the respondents’ support preferences using the Chi-Squared test and ANOVA. A statistically significant preference for functional support was identified in the sexual abuse and peer pressure scenarios and among those willing to help in the peer pressure scenario. Qualitative analysis of functional support preference focused on actionable guidance. Our findings revealed support preferences and design implications for chatbots. These findings indicate a priority for utility and safety and utility over sentiment. We conclude with trauma-informed design recommendations.

items.title: Games People Play: Strategies to Develop and Release Online Games
items.abstract: When should a game studio continue building in beta and when should it go live? In an industry defined by continuous updates and diverse players, online game developers must decide what to build and when to release while balancing engagement, monetization, and development resources. Unlike traditional software, online games operate in a mass market environment where users differ widely in experience and tolerance for bugs, and where frequent updates are essential to maintain interest and competitiveness. We show that beta releases are not only testing tools but strategic instruments for managing user diversity, product complexity, and release timing. Beta phases allow firms to gather feedback and refine features before broader release. Full releases should be delayed when complexity is high or when experienced users represent a large share of the user base. Release decisions must balance development constraints with market pressures. Although delaying releases can improve quality, competition may require earlier launches. From a policy perspective, platform operators can support better outcomes by enabling structured beta programs, managing user expectations, and providing tools for staged rollouts. These practices help improve product quality, reduce negative user experiences, and enhance long-term user engagement in digital ecosystems.

items.title: Hazard perception in manual and hands-off Level 2 driving under daytime and after dark lighting conditions: A driving simulator study
items.abstract: The aim of this study was to examine drivers' hazard perception in an urban scene, under two different lighting conditions (daytime and after dark) and for two different levels of driving automation (manual driving and hands-off SAE level 2 automation). Forty-eight participants took part in four experimental drives in a driving simulator, encountering six different hazardous/potentially hazardous events in each drive. Results showed that drivers detected hazards significantly earlier and were more likely to react to the hazards in daytime, compared to after dark environments, particularly when pedestrians were approaching the road from the left. However, there was no significant difference in their response time towards the hazards, between the daytime and after dark environments. In terms of driver response in the two automation levels, the majority of drivers were proactive and reacted before the potentially hazardous events turned into actual hazards during manual driving, but responses were more reactive during automated driving. These findings highlight the need to account for context of the driving environment such as lighting conditions and levels of driving automation when designing systems or protocols that aim to support hazard perception and timely driver response.

The experiment employed a 2 (time pressure: with vs. without) × 2 (AI role: expert vs. assistant) within-subjects design, measuring perceived self-capability, perceived AI capability, compliance, and electroencephalography (EEG) activity during the task.ResultsTime pressure and AI role influenced compliance through relative advantage (perceived AI capability minus perceived self-capability). Higher relative advantage values predicted higher compliance rates.ConclusionFindings across different time pressures and AI role support Relative Advantage Theory, which provides a potential explanation for inconsistencies reported in prior studies.ApplicationThe findings offer theoretical insights for designing AI systems optimized for emergency use.

items.title: Impact of individual factors on stepping anomalies in ladder climbing
items.abstract: Preventing occupational falls from ladders is impeded by a limited understanding of how ladder design and the climber influence motor errors and compensation strategies during climbing. This study identified relationships between individual factors, ladder design, and destabilizing and compensatory events across 87 individuals. We assessed the impact of grip strength, waist-to-height ratio (WHR) and ladder angle on four common events: rung kicking, foot readjustments, double stepping (stepping on a rung with both feet), and skipping rungs. Events occurred in 21.5% of trials. Rung kicks were associated with vertical ladders and ascent, whereas foot readjustments were associated with vertical ladders and descent. High grip strength and low WHR were associated with skipping rungs, but low strength and high WHR were associated with double stepping. Thus, ladder fall risk was dependent on the ladder (with non-vertical ladders improving safety) and the individual (where leaner climbers and greater strength were safer). • Destabilizing and compensatory events are common during ladder use. • More destabilizing events occur on vertically oriented ladders. • Rung kicks and foot readjustments are associated with the ladder design and task. • Double stepping and skipping rungs are associated with strength and obesity.

items.title: Internet use, social isolation, and loneliness among older adults: A multi-wave analysis
items.abstract: This study investigated the longitudinal relationship between the frequency of internet use and loneliness in older adults in the UK, considering perceived social isolation. Data were obtained from Waves 9-14 of the UK Household Longitudinal Study. Linear mixed models were employed to examine the association between internet use, loneliness, and social isolation over time. The analytical sample comprised 13,704 adults aged 65 and above. The models controlled for sociodemographic and health-related covariates. The results suggested that infrequent internet users (including those with no internet access) experienced higher levels of loneliness compared to frequent internet users, especially daily users. The associations persisted even after adjusting the models for covariates. Participants who frequently felt socially isolated consistently reported the highest levels of loneliness, regardless of their level of digital engagement. A significant three-way interaction between wave, internet use, and social isolation revealed that differences between the socially isolated and non-isolated older adults were the largest during Waves 11-13 and narrowed by Wave 14. This shift may be an outcome of COVID-19, reflecting the pandemic’s lasting social impact. These findings support the Digital Divide framework. The frequency of internet use is associated with lower levels of loneliness in older adults who do not feel socially isolated; however, internet use alone may not be enough to fill the void of human interaction in those who feel socially isolated.

items.title: Passive Construction Site Safety Monitoring via Persona-Scaffolded Adversarial Chain-of-Thought VLM Verification
items.abstract: Construction remains the deadliest industry sector in the United States, with 1,055 fatal worker injuries recorded in 2023, and the majority preventable. Existing monitoring approaches are expensive, require real-time human operators, or address only a narrow subset of violations. This paper presents a passive, end-of-shift construction safety monitoring pipeline processing video from POV body-worn and fixed wall-mounted cameras through a three-stage architecture: (1) fine-tuned YOLO11 for primary PPE and hazard detection, (2) SAM 3 for segmentation refinement and worker deduplication, and (3) Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with a method-prompted, persona-scaffolded three-pass adversarial chain-of-thought protocol for compliance verification and hallucination control. The principal contribution is the Stage 3 prompt design: professional persona backstories following the method-actor framing drive an observed 12% precision improvement over single-pass prompting in an informal three-author review of the 12-video Ironsite development corpus, with the largest gains on hallucination-prone violation categories. Structural message isolation enforces observational independence between a generator, discriminator, and reconciliation pass governed by asymmetric rules encoding priors about human observation versus automated detection reliability. The system maps violations to OSHA standards, performs REBA-inspired ergonomic risk scoring from pose keypoints, and produces per-worker safety reports with timestamped evidence. An evaluation harness is released for future reproduction.

items.title: Prebunking false information in the wild: Do inoculation-based interventions work against real-world false information?
items.abstract: In recent years, various interventions have been developed to reduce individuals’ susceptibility to false and misleading content. Among these, inoculation-based interventions—which preemptively expose people to common manipulation techniques to reduce their susceptibility to falsehoods—have gained popularity in both academic and applied settings, including public education campaigns and platform-level deployments. However, most evaluations have been conducted in controlled settings where each falsehood contains a single manipulation technique, raising concerns about their ecological validity. To inform more robust intervention design, we present two complementary studies that examine the limitations of current inoculation interventions. Study 1 analyzes large-scale COVID-19 and Non-COVID false information datasets to assess the prevalence, co-occurrence, and virality of manipulation techniques, and finds that current interventions rely on oversimplified assumptions about the structure of false information. Study 2 tests whether inoculation against single-technique (emotional language) transfers to multi-technique false information (e.g., emotional language & polarization), and shows its transferability is limited. Taken together, these findings highlight the need to re-evaluate how prevailing inoculation-based interventions are designed and to better adapt them to the complexity of real-world false information environments.

items.title: Risk Management in Aviation: Safety, Regulation, and Crisis Prevention
items.abstract: Aviation, as one of the most complex and high-risk industries, demands meticulous risk management strategies to ensure passenger safety, operational efficiency, and regulatory compliance. This book delves into the fundamental principles of risk assessment in the aviation sector, addressing the multifaceted challenges of safety protocols, stringent regulatory frameworks, and crisis prevention mechanisms. By exploring historical aviation incidents, modern technological advancements, and evolving safety regulations, the book provides a comprehensive perspective on mitigating operational risks. It underscores the critical role of global regulatory bodies, aviation safety management systems, and the integration of advanced analytics in predicting and preventing crises. Through an interdisciplinary approach, this work offers valuable insights for industry professionals, policymakers, and academics seeking to enhance aviation safety standards. With a combination of theoretical discourse and real-world case studies, the book serves as an essential guide for navigating the complexities of risk management in contemporary aviation. The rapid expansion of the global aviation industry has brought unprecedented challenges in maintaining safety, adhering to regulatory requirements, and preventing crises. While technological advancements have significantly improved aircraft reliability and operational efficiency, the inherent risks associated with aviation remain a pressing concern. The increasing complexity of air traffic management, environmental factors, and human error further contribute to the vulnerabilities within the industry. This book was written to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding and managing risks in aviation. It bridges the gap between theoretical principles and practical applications by examining key safety measures, international regulatory structures, and crisis management strategies. The work is grounded in real-world case studies and empirical research, ensuring that readers gain a nuanced perspective on mitigating aviation risks effectively. Risk management in aviation refers to the systematic approach of identifying, assessing, and mitigating potential hazards that could compromise safety, operational continuity, and regulatory compliance. This involves proactive planning, continuous monitoring, and implementing best practices in aviation safety. Fundamental concepts in this field include hazard identification, which focuses on detecting potential risks before they escalate; risk assessment, which evaluates the probability and impact of identified hazards; safety management systems (SMS), which provide structured procedures for handling risks; and regulatory compliance, which ensures that aviation stakeholders adhere to international safety guidelines set by organizations such as the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Several critical phenomena have shaped the evolution of risk management in aviation. The increasing volume of air traffic has heightened the potential for mid-air collisions, runway incursions, and airspace congestion. Climate change has introduced additional risks, such as extreme weather conditions, turbulence, and increased susceptibility to lightning strikes. Moreover, cybersecurity threats have become a growing concern, with modern aircraft relying extensively on digital systems that are vulnerable to cyberattacks. Human factors also play a significant role, as pilot fatigue, communication breakdowns, and decision-making errors remain key contributors to aviation incidents. Understanding these phenomena is essential for developing robust mitigation strategies. Aviation risk management operates on several core principles. The precautionary principle emphasizes the importance of taking preventive measures even in the absence of complete scientific certainty. Continuous improvement ensures that risk management strategies evolve in response to emerging threats and technological advancements. Another fundamental principle is integrated safety management, which requires seamless collaboration between airlines, airports, regulatory agencies, and maintenance teams. Additionally, data-driven decision-making allows aviation stakeholders to leverage big data and artificial intelligence to predict and mitigate risks effectively. Several indicators help assess risk levels in aviation. Incident and accident rates provide quantitative measurements of safety performance. Operational disruptions, such as flight delays and emergency landings, highlight areas where risk mitigation strategies may need improvement. Other indicators include pilot error rates, which assess the frequency of human-related mistakes, and aircraft maintenance records, which track the reliability and condition of aviation equipment. Safety audits and compliance assessments also serve as essential tools in evaluating risk exposure. Effective aviation risk management relies on several operational variables, including regulatory policies, which define safety standards and procedures; technological advancements, which introduce new tools for hazard detection and mitigation; and human factors, which influence pilot performance and decision-making. Environmental conditions, such as weather patterns and airspace congestion, also play a crucial role in determining aviation risks. Additionally, financial considerations impact the allocation of resources toward safety enhancements and crisis response initiatives. Several factors determine the effectiveness of aviation risk management. The level of regulatory enforcement influences how strictly safety measures are implemented across the industry. Technological integration determines the efficiency of hazard detection and mitigation. Corporate safety culture also plays a vital role, as organizations that prioritize safety over financial considerations tend to experience fewer incidents. Furthermore, international cooperation is essential, given the global nature of air travel and the need for uniform safety standards across different regions. Successful implementation of aviation risk management strategies requires a multi-layered approach. This involves incorporating predictive analytics to anticipate potential threats, enhancing pilot training programs to minimize human errors, and investing in resilient aviation infrastructure to withstand environmental and operational challenges. Collaboration between government agencies, airlines, and technological innovators is crucial to ensuring that risk management frameworks remain effective. Additionally, crisis response protocols must be regularly updated to adapt to evolving threats. Aviation risk management faces numerous challenges, including resistance to regulatory changes, financial constraints, and the unpredictability of emerging threats such as cyberattacks and pandemics. The rapid pace of technological advancement also presents difficulties in ensuring that safety regulations keep up with innovations. However, several factors support the effectiveness of risk management in aviation. Increased investments in aviation safety research, the implementation of automated monitoring systems, and international collaboration among regulatory bodies contribute to the continuous improvement of risk mitigation strategies. Risk management in aviation is a dynamic and multifaceted discipline that requires a proactive, data-driven, and collaborative approach. By understanding the complex interplay of safety regulations, technological advancements, and human factors, aviation stakeholders can work toward minimizing risks and ensuring the highest standards of safety. This book provides a comprehensive examination of aviation risk management, offering valuable insights for industry professionals, policymakers, and academics. By integrating real-world case studies, theoretical frameworks, and strategic recommendations, it serves as a definitive guide for navigating the complexities of aviation safety and crisis prevention.

items.title: The Dual Role of Individualism in AI Chatbot Disclosure: How Privacy Concerns, Culture, and Behavior Shape Human–AI Communication Across Mainland China, Germany, Japan, Hong Kong, and the U.S.
items.abstract: The privacy–disclosure relationship is often treated as uniform and cross-culturally stable. This study challenges this assumption by surveying N = 5,096 AI chatbot users in Mainland China, Germany, Hong Kong, Japan, and the U.S. Results show substantial, cross-cultural differences in self-disclosure across breadth, depth, honesty, and valence with Chinese users disclosing most and German users least. Privacy concerns reduced honesty and valence, but not breadth or depth. Multilevel models revealed that individual-level behavioral individualism increased self-disclosure but also strengthened the negative link between privacy concerns and disclosure honesty. In contrast, cultural individualism reduced self-disclosure overall but buffered the negative association between privacy concerns and all disclosure dimensions. These findings complicate the presumed uniform role of individualism in privacy behavior and extend Communication Privacy Management theory by integrating both micro- and macro-level cultural contingencies in human–AI interactions. Implications for culturally adaptive, privacy-conscious AI design are discussed.

items.title: The Dynamics of Attention Across Automated and Manual Driving Modes: A Driving Simulation Study
items.abstract: ObjectiveThis study aims to explore the dynamics of driver attention to various zones, including road, central mirror, center stack, and instrument cluster, across different driving modes in AVs.BackgroundThe integration of automated vehicles (AVs) into transportation systems has introduced critical safety concerns, particularly regarding driver re-engagement during mode transitions. Past crashes underscore the risks when drivers overly rely on automation and highlight the need to understand dynamic attention allocation to support safety during automated driving.MethodA high-fidelity driving simulation was conducted to examine drivers' visual attention. Eye-tracking technology was employed to measure fixation duration, fixation count, and time to first fixation (TFF) across distinct driving modes (automated, manual, and transition). These indicators were analyzed to capture both sustained attention (fixation duration/count) and attentional reallocation/latency (time to first fixation), which are the critical aspects of visual attention to different areas of interest (AOIs).ResultsFindings show that drivers' attention varies significantly across driving modes. In manual mode, attention consistently focuses on the road, while in automated mode, prolonged fixation on center stack was observed. During the handover and takeover phases, attention shifts dynamically between environmental and technological elements.ConclusionThe study reveals that driver attention allocation is mode dependent. These findings inform the design of center stacks in AVs that align with drivers' attention patterns. By presenting relevant information according to the driving context, such systems can enhance driver-vehicle interaction, support effective transitions, and improve overall safety.ApplicationSystematic analysis of visual attention dynamics across driving modes is gaining prominence, as it informs center stack designs and driver readiness interventions. The generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) findings can be directly applied to the design of center stack or driver training programs to enhance attention and improve safety.

items.title: User Experience Analysis and Design Strategies for Improving Online Medical Consultation Processes for Older Adults: A Case Study of Ping An Good Doctor
items.abstract: This study examines how older adults engage with online medical consultation workflows and identifies key usability barriers that limit their access to digital healthcare services. Drawing on Garrett’s Five Elements of User Experience as an analytical framework, the research combines semi-structured interviews (N = 15), task-based user testing, and System Usability Scale (SUS) evaluation to explore issues related to navigation, cognitive load, AI triage, and trust in the Ping An Good Doctor app. The results indicate that multilayered task flows, text-input burdens, unclear physician credentials, and inconsistent interaction cues disproportionately affect users aged 70 and above. Based on these findings, a redesigned prototype was developed, incorporating dual-entry navigation, a simplified task structure, voice-assisted input, enhanced credential visibility, and age-friendly visual adjustments. Usability improved substantially, with the average SUS score increasing from 60.4 to 75.0. The study offers a user experience (UX)-oriented optimization framework that may inform the design of age-friendly mobile healthcare consultation systems.

items.title: Using Biometrics to Understand AI-Assisted Coding Performance and its Perception
items.abstract: AI-based code assistants are transforming software development, yet we lack empirical evidence on how they affect developers' cognitive processes. We present a multisite study investigating the neurophysiological correlates of AI-assisted programming through a within-subjects crossover design. We recruited participants at two universities (Bari, Italy, and Copenhagen, Denmark) and collected electroencephalography, eye-tracking, electrodermal activity, and heart rate variability data alongside a rubric-based performance score and self-reported workload across six dimensions using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). We tested four hypotheses addressing physiological differences between AI-assisted and non-assisted conditions, the moderating role of developer experience, the association between physiology and performance, and the alignment between subjective perceptions and objective measures. Under AI assistance, the EEG $θ/α$ ratio was lower during the first task and the gaze blink rate was higher during the second, both consistent with reduced cognitive engagement when developers offload generative effort to the model. This pattern did not differ between undergraduate and graduate students. Electrodermal activity correlated with performance under the non-AI condition but not under AI. Among the six NASA-TLX dimensions of self-reported workload, only Physical demand was associated with performance under the non-AI condition but not under AI. These findings suggest that AI-assisted programming is not a faster version of solo coding but a cognitively distinct activity, with implications for the design of AI assistants and for biometric monitoring in AI-augmented development.

items.title: “I Started to Actually Develop Confidence”: A Controlled Usability Study of a Personal Informatics Tool for Supporting Online News Content Discernment Among Young Adults
items.abstract: Readers today face increasing challenges in distinguishing genuine news from misinformation and identifying biased content within algorithmically curated media environments. While prior research has focused on automated detection and adjustments to news recommendation systems, less attention has been given to user-facing interventions that shape how individuals engage with news. To address this gap, we introduce a browser-based personal informatics dashboard designed to support online news consumption by increasing awareness of bias, source quality, and credibility. In a between-subjects study (n = 100), our tool improved users’ ability to identify false information and encouraged more active engagement with news content (p < 0.05). We also observed increased lateral reading behaviors, such as cross-checking sources, suggesting deeper critical engagement. Findings are based on an integrated set of intervention features and combine statistical analyses with exploratory insights into user behavior. By adopting a personal informatics perspective, this work shifts focus from passive misinformation detection toward active, user-centered media literacy and more reflective interaction with news.

items.title: “This Is My Book!”: An AI-Enabled Reading Intervention System and Design Principles for Chinese Children With Dyslexia
items.abstract: Chinese children with dyslexia face persistent deficits in character recognition and fluency, yet existing interventions often lack personalization and accessibility. We present ReadCraft, an AI-enabled reading intervention system transforming children from passive readers into active creators. ReadCraft employs a novel Create-Read-Produce framework: children first co-create stories via three AI-assisted modes, then engage in four graded reading practice modes ranging from AI mentorship to independent challenges, and finally produce complete books with custom illustrations. Evaluated in a controlled study with 52 children, the system demonstrated significant improvements in reading accuracy, fluency, motivation, and self-efficacy compared to traditional materials. Qualitative insights from multi-stakeholder interviews further validated the system’s efficacy. Based on these empirical findings, we derive a set of actionable design principles for developing inclusive, AI-powered reading tools. This research demonstrates how AI-enabled personalized creation can bridge the gap between motivation and remediation in special education.

items.title: AI as the mirror, mate, and mentor: negotiating romantic relationships with ChatGPT as “Teacher G” on Xiaohongshu
items.abstract: Abstract How are artificial intelligence technologies transforming human experiences of romance and intimacy in the digital age? So far, human-AI romantic relationships have primarily been studied in the context of AI models designed explicitly for emotional companionship (e.g., Replika). This study focuses on users’ engagement with general-purpose AI systems like ChatGPT. It explores how female users on Xiaohongshu (i.e., RedNote) discursively construct ChatGPT as “Teacher G,” a form of address that merges romantic interest with pedagogical authority to negotiate AI-mediated intimacy. Through critical discourse analysis of user-generated posts, we identify three roles users assign to ChatGPT: a mirror for self-reflection, a mate fulfilling relational desires, and a mentor guiding self-acceptance and personal growth. Findings show that users actively appropriate AI for self-exploration with clear metacognitive awareness of projection. In its mentor role, the AI fosters reflexive self-awareness by guiding autonomy in social contexts, encouraging self-acceptance, and supporting the renegotiation rather than the transcendence of relational boundaries through individual and communal reflection. Yet this process can also reproduce patriarchal authority, particularly when users seek validation for conforming to feminine norms, encouraging dependence on an authoritative persona. This duality positions human-AI intimacy as a sociotechnical practice where users navigate self-discipline within persistent cultural constraints, highlighting the co-constitution of technology and social norms. We argue that future AI design should center on user empowerment while critically accounting for cultural contexts rather than relying on prescriptive relational scripts.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Alliances, and Innovation1
items.abstract: This paper examines the influence of artificial intelligence (AI) on research and development (R&D) practices, proposing that AI enables firms to discover, evaluate, and make sense of information from their partners, thereby reducing information asymmetry and allowing alliances to flourish. Empirically, we approximate a firm’s AI resources using patents and job postings to analyze the relationship amongst AI, alliances, and drug innovation in the pharmaceutical industry. Our findings show that firms with greater AI resources shift their locus of innovation toward alliances and develop more drugs from their alliances. Furthermore, AI can be particularly useful in exploiting information held by counterparties within an alliance. Taken together, our study highlights the complementary role of AI and alliances, shedding light on how modern organizational and technological advancements jointly shape the production of innovation.

items.title: Assessing Localization Technologies for Pedestrian Collision Avoidance
items.abstract: Robust pedestrian safety is crucial to the next-generation of intelligent transportation systems. Such systems rely on active pedestrian localization and predictive collision alerts. Pedestrian localization can be supported by Ultra-Wideband technology and Bluetooth 6.0, which offer high-precision ranging and low-latency communication, making them promising candidates for vehicular collision warning systems. This paper assesses the localization accuracy of these technologies for pedestrian alerting and benchmarks their performance against Global Navigation Satellite Systems. Experimental evaluations performed in this paper focused on key performance metrics, including localization accuracy and robustness to environmental conditions. Preliminary results suggest that Ultra-Wideband and Bluetooth 6.0 can serve as viable alternatives or complements to Global Navigation Satellite Systems in certain scenarios, improving situational awareness and enabling timely pedestrian alerts.

items.title: Attention Restoration and Mental Imagery in Direct and Indirect Biophilic VR Retail Environments: An Eye-Tracking Study
items.abstract: This study explores how biophilic design cues in virtual reality (VR) interfaces influence users’ visual attention, restorative experience, and mental imagery. Using a between-subjects experimental design, a VR-based eye-tracking experiment was conducted in immersive retail environments featuring either direct biophilic design (authentic natural elements) or indirect biophilic design (nature-inspired graphics). We designated two areas of interest (biophilic background and product area in a store) to capture participants’ gaze behavior. According to the correlation analysis, fixation and saccade metrics were associated with four restorative experience dimensions, mental imagery fluency, and shopping satisfaction. In the direct biophilic condition, saccades across background and product areas increased mental imagery fluency as well as the restorative experience to enhance satisfaction. In the indirect design environment, mental imagery mediated the relationship between restorative experience and satisfaction. The present study offers implications for VR designs that facilitate restorative experience and mental simulation to improve user experiences.

items.title: Attributions about organizational motives behind wellness programs: An employee-centered approach.
items.abstract: Using a human resource (HR) attributions lens, we uncover 16 attributions that employees make about the reasons why their organization provides wellness programs. We also examine the implications of such attributions for employee outcomes (i.e., psychological strain, job burnout, job satisfaction). Recognizing employees can hold multiple HR attributions at the same time, an employee-centered approach was used. Through latent profile analysis with a sample of 517 Australian employees, four wellness program attribution profiles emerged: indifferent, favorable, unfavorable and ambivalent. Overall, employees with a favorable profile of wellness program attributions experienced better health and well-being outcomes compared to those with an unfavorable profile. In addition, employees in the unfavorable profile were found to have higher psychological strain, higher job burnout, and lower job satisfaction compared with their indifferent counterparts. Furthermore, employees with a profile of unfavorable attributions had higher psychological strain and lower job satisfaction compared to those with more mixed views about their wellness program. Past participation was unrelated to employee outcomes, but past participation predicted profile membership, suggesting that it is the attributions employees hold about their wellness programs that matter more than actual usage. Overall, we advance our understanding of HR attributions within the specific context of wellness programs and offer novel insights into a far greater number of attributions than previously studied for any HR practice.
